explanation:
[FEATURE: hr]
[EFFECT] Hour of day has a strongly non-monotonic, double-peaked effect. Demand is at its lowest in the very early morning (around 4 a.m., where the contribution is deeply negative), then rises sharply to a morning commuter peak at 8 a.m. It dips slightly through midday, then climbs to the highest point of the day at 5 p.m. (17:00), before falling steadily through the evening back to overnight lows.
[IMPORTANCE] This is by far the most important feature (rank 1), with an importance score nearly three and a half times larger than the next feature — it dominates the model's predictions more than all other features combined.

[FEATURE: temp]
[EFFECT] Warmer temperatures consistently raise predicted demand. The effect rises steeply from very cold conditions (around 1 °C, where contribution is strongly negative) up through mild and warm temperatures, peaking around 30–31 °C. Beyond that, at extreme heat (close to 40 °C), the contribution dips slightly back toward zero, suggesting a small reduction at very high temperatures.
[IMPORTANCE] This is the second most important feature (rank 2) — a meaningful driver, though its influence is roughly one-third the size of the hour-of-day effect.

[FEATURE: yr]
[EFFECT] This feature captures a year-over-year growth trend: 2011 carries a negative contribution (reducing predicted demand) while 2012 carries a positive one, reflecting that the bike-share system grew significantly between the two years. The effect behaves like a step change between the two years.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked third in importance, this feature has a moderately strong effect — slightly smaller than temperature but clearly meaningful for baseline demand levels.

[FEATURE: mnth]
[EFFECT] Month has a non-monotonic effect. Winter months (January and February) suppress demand noticeably, spring and summer months are closer to neutral, and the autumn months — particularly October — produce the highest positive contribution. October is the peak month, with September and November also positive, while July and August are surprisingly close to neutral or slightly negative.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked fourth, month has a moderate effect, roughly one-third the size of temperature's influence, and plays a secondary seasonal-adjustment role on top of temperature.

[FEATURE: hum]
[EFFECT] Humidity has a predominantly negative effect at high levels. At moderate humidity (roughly 30–40%), the contribution is slightly positive, but as humidity climbs above about 70–75%, the contribution turns negative and continues declining, reaching its most suppressive values near 100% humidity. Very low humidity (below ~10%) also shows a negative value, though this may reflect very few such observations.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked fifth, humidity has a modest but real effect — smaller than month, and most noticeable at the high end of the humidity range where it noticeably reduces predicted demand.

[FEATURE: weathersit]
[EFFECT] Clear weather (category 1) gives a small positive boost to demand; mist or cloud (category 2) is essentially neutral. Light rain or snow (category 3) produces the sharpest drop in predicted demand. Interestingly, heavy rain (category 4) shows a slightly less negative contribution than light rain, though this may reflect very few heavy-rain observations in the data.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked sixth, weather situation has a moderate impact — mainly felt when conditions deteriorate to rain or snow, where it meaningfully cuts predicted rentals.

[FEATURE: weekday]
[EFFECT] The day of the week has a small effect across its range. Sunday shows the most negative contribution, demand edges upward through the working week, and Friday has the highest contribution. Saturday is slightly below Friday. The total spread from Sunday to Friday is small (roughly 0.10 in log terms).
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked seventh, weekday has a low importance — it matters, but only slightly, and should not be a primary planning focus.

[FEATURE: windspeed]
[EFFECT] At low to moderate wind speeds the contribution is close to zero or marginally positive, meaning wind has little effect under normal conditions. However, at high wind speeds (above roughly 30 km/h, normalised value ~0.45) the contribution becomes increasingly negative, reaching its most suppressive values at the highest recorded wind speeds (around 55 km/h).
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked eighth, windspeed has a low overall importance — its effect is negligible for most hours and only becomes relevant during notably windy conditions.

[FEATURE: holiday]
[EFFECT] Being a holiday produces a small negative contribution to predicted demand compared with a normal working day, which is near zero. The effect is a simple step: non-holidays are essentially neutral and holidays slightly reduce the model's prediction.
[IMPORTANCE] Ranked last (ninth) with the lowest importance score — its effect is negligible and should not meaningfully influence operational planning on its own.

[RECOMMENDATION] Plan your bike availability and staffing primarily around the hour of the day — ensuring high fleet availability and staff support around the 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. peaks — and secondarily around temperature, scaling up resources on warm days (around 20–31 °C) and scaling back on cold or very rainy days.
